column4: The section pictures a weak person needing support; this ayah recalls the Prophet as an orphan whom God sheltered, فَآوَىٰ, a direct instance of aid given to vulnerability.
The section names root ه د ي for guidance and describes the lost, wavering traveler; this ayah says God found the Prophet lost and guided him, فَهَدَىٰ.
The section's weak traveler asks for help; this ayah says God found the Prophet in need and enriched him, وَوَجَدَكَ عَائِلًا فَأَغْنَىٰ.
The section names root ه د ي and pictures someone too weak to proceed alone; this ayah describes people unable to devise a way or find a path, وَلَا يَهْتَدُونَ سَبِيلًا.
Oppressed men, women, and children cry to God to bring them out and appoint a protector and helper; their explicit plea for rescue and backing closely matches the section's support-seeking traveler.
The section links bodily support with standing upright; here God makes the youths' hearts firm, وَرَبَطْنَا عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمْ, when they rise, إِذْ قَامُوا, to declare their faith.
The section's dictionary sense *qiyām* is a support that prevents collapse; this ayah says God holds the sky lest it fall upon earth, وَيُمْسِكُ السَّمَاءَ أَن تَقَعَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ.
The section's root ع و ن appears again in وَاسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّبْرِ وَالصَّلَاةِ; this repeated command names patience and prayer as aid to seek and adds God's presence with the patient.
Ibrahim and Ismail raise the House's foundations, يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ الْقَوَاعِدَ, then ask God to accept their work; two people build a lasting support and turn to God for aid.
The youths ask God for mercy and sound direction in their affair, رَشَدًا; their plea for right guidance in a vulnerable situation meets the section's request for help and a way.
The section names root ع ب د through *na'budu* and defines help as what one relies on; this ayah asks whether God is not sufficient for His servant, أَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ بِكَافٍ عَبْدَهُ.
The section asks for guidance; Moses asks to follow a teacher so he may learn right direction, رُشْدًا, directly presenting a seeker asking to be led and taught.
The section joins worship and asking for help; this ayah says to seek provision from God, فَابْتَغُوا عِندَ اللَّهِ الرِّزْقَ, and worship Him, فَاعْبُدُوهُ.
The section begins with a traveler stranded when his mount fails; this ayah promises a migrant many places of refuge and ample provision, مُرَاغَمًا كَثِيرًا وَسَعَةً.
The section describes a wall about to fall and then repaired; this parable contrasts a building founded on reverence with one on the edge of a crumbling bank that collapses, فَانْهَارَ بِهِ.

The section's dictionary form *qiyām* is a visible prop or support; this ayah describes the heavens raised without pillars that people can see, بِغَيْرِ عَمَدٍ تَرَوْنَهَا, a specific boundary between visible props and unseen support.

The section's dictionary form *qiyām* is a prop; this repeated creation description says the heavens have no visible pillars, بِغَيْرِ عَمَدٍ تَرَوْنَهَا, while firm mountains keep the earth from shaking.
The section's story uses قوّة as strength lent to build a protective barrier; here the same word names military force prepared to deter enemies, a specific different use of strength.
These people say they were oppressed and weak in the land; the next ayah, 4:98, specifies those unable to find a way, completing the picture of people whose movement is constrained.
The section makes the traveler's dependence visible; this ayah states the specific relation beneath it: people are فقَرَاءُ إِلَى اللَّهِ, in need of God, while He is free of need.
The section's traveler needs ground on which to stand and walk; this ayah describes earth as a مِهَادًا, a resting-place prepared for people.
The section's dictionary examples use roots and supports to keep something upright; this ayah calls mountains أَوْتَادًا, pegs that secure a structure.
The section names root ق و م and glosses *qiyām* as support; this ayah uses قَوَّامُونَ for a sustaining role tied in its own wording to spending, a social form of support.
The section hears bodily uprightness in root ق و م and joins it to worship; the command قُمِ اللَّيْلَ calls the Prophet to rise for night devotion.
The section's dictionary form says a mount may *qāmat* when it tires and stops moving; here people walk when light appears but قَامُوا when darkness returns, a halt on an uncertain route.

At the well, two women hold back their flock because they cannot water it until the shepherds leave and their father is old; 28:24 adds Moses' practical help, while this ayah itself establishes their need.
After Moses' prayer for good in 28:24, one woman comes to him walking with modesty and conveys her father's invitation; this ayah depicts help arriving through another person.
The woman describes Moses as strong and trustworthy and proposes hiring him; after the need and invitation in 28:23–25, this ayah's own contribution is a practical offer of support through work.
After the foundation-building in 2:127, Ibrahim and Ismail ask God to show them their rites, وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَا; this ayah's own contribution is a request for guidance in worship.
After the collapsing-building parable in 9:109, this ayah says the building they made remains a source of doubt in their hearts; it completes the scene with the structure's lasting inner effect.
Moses prays, رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي, asking for his chest to be opened; the section's support image is bodily, and this is a specific request for inward capacity.
Moses asks, وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي, for his task to be made easy; this is a direct request for help to proceed, joined to the bodily plea in 20:25.
The prayer asks for truthful entry and exit and for a supporting authority from God, سُلْطَانًا نَّصِيرًا; it joins movement along a way with requested backing.
The section names root ق و م in *mustaqīm*; this command calls God's route the straight path, صِرَاطِي مُسْتَقِيمًا, and warns against side paths that divide the traveler.

The section names roots ه د ي and ق و م in asking for guidance to the straight path; this ayah says God guides people through paths of peace and to a straight path, وَيَهْدِيهِمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.
The ayah includes the wayfarer, وَابْنَ السَّبِيلِ, among those who receive wealth in a definition of righteousness; it gives the stranded traveler's need a concrete place in the community's care.
Believing men and women are described as allies of one another, أَوْلِيَاءُ بَعْضٍ; this is a specific communal counterpart to the two people supporting the weak walker.
The section names root ه د ي for guidance; Ibrahim says he is going to his Lord and He will guide him, إِنِّي ذَاهِبٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ, joining travel with reliance on guidance.

The section's dictionary form *tehādī* describes swaying from side to side; people here appear intoxicated from terror, though they are not. The ayah does not say they walk, so the visual resemblance is uncertain.
